## Worldview
Vienna is the residence of Emperor Leopold I and a city of the Counter-Reformation: the university is run by the Jesuits, books are censored, the Jews were expelled in 1670 and Protestants are barely tolerated. Learned medicine is still Galenic, with chemical remedies and the circulation of the blood accepted by some; plague (the city lost many thousands in 1679) is explained by corrupted air, contagion through goods and persons, and God's punishment for sin. Astronomy is taught after Tycho, not Copernicus. The new experimental philosophy of London, Paris and the Dutch towns (air pump, barometer, microscope, pendulum clock) is known here from Latin books and Jesuit compendia rather than practised. Craft knowledge is strong: gun founders, clockmakers, apothecaries, miners from the Habsburg lands. In June 1683 an Ottoman army is marching on the city, whose fortifications have been neglected.

## People
- **Paul de Sorbait**: professor of anatomy and medical practice at the university, physician to the Empress Dowager Eleonore, Generalinquisitor in plague matters in 1679. Knows: Galenic and newer medicine, plague management, anatomy (doctorate Padua 1652); member of the Leopoldina since 1672. — In Vienna. Aged 59, stays through the siege as Oberstwachtmeister of the academic legion and later commands its 3rd company. Dies 1691.
- **Leopold Karl von Kollonitsch**: Bishop of Wiener Neustadt since 1670, former Knight of Malta who fought at Candia (1651) and the Dardanelles (1655). Knows: siege experience, raising money, organising care. — Comes from Wiener Neustadt into the besieged city, pays the troops, sets up emergency hospitals in monasteries, and after the relief cares for about 500 orphans at Mailberg.
- **Abraham a Sancta Clara**: Discalced Augustinian, imperial court preacher since 1677, author of Mercks Wienn (1680) on the plague. Knows: preaching, the plague year 1679 from inside Vienna, popular opinion. — Not in Vienna. Transferred to Graz in 1682 and preaches there in 1683; publishes Auff, auff, ihr Christen against the Turks that year.
- **Johann Andreas von Liebenberg**: Mayor of Vienna since 1679. Knows: city administration, the citizen companies, provisioning. — In Vienna; directs the citizens' fortification work and militia. Falls ill in August, with Daniel Fockhy as his deputy, and dies of dysentery on 9 September 1683.
- **Antonie van Leeuwenhoek**: draper and municipal official at Delft, Fellow of the Royal Society since 1680. Knows: single-lens microscopes; animalcules in water (1674–1676), spermatozoa (1677), bacteria from teeth (letter of 17 September 1683). — In Delft. Reachable only by letter, writes Dutch only, and shows visitors his lesser lenses.
- **Francesco Redi**: chief physician to the Medici court in Florence. Knows: experiments against spontaneous generation (1668), parasites (book of 1684), viper venom. — In Florence; reachable by letter through Italian and Jesuit channels.
- **Matthäus Gottfried Purmann**: surgeon at Halberstadt, plague surgeon there in 1680. Knows: field surgery (Der rechte und wahrhafftige Feldscher, 1680), plague buboes, failed lamb's-blood transfusions. — At Halberstadt in 1683; moves to Breslau in 1685.
- **Johann Kunckel**: chymist and glassmaker to the Elector of Brandenburg at Potsdam. Knows: phosphorus, gold ruby glass, glass recipes (Ars Vitraria Experimentalis, 1679). — At Potsdam and Berlin; reachable by letter or a journey of several weeks; guards his recipes.
- **Wolf Helmhard von Hohberg**: Lower Austrian nobleman and writer on estate farming, Protestant exile at Regensburg. Knows: Austrian agriculture, vineyards, ponds and household economy (Georgica curiosa, 1682). — Lives at Regensburg, up the Danube, since 1664; dies there in 1688.
- **Luigi Ferdinando Marsigli**: Bolognese nobleman, engineer officer in imperial service, naturalist. Knows: Ottoman army and customs, fortification, coffee, the currents of the Bosporus (book of 1681). — Wounded and captured on the Raab in early July 1683, sold to a pasha and made to brew coffee in the Ottoman camp before Vienna; freed in 1684.
- **Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz**: court councillor and librarian of the Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg at Hanover. Knows: calculus (unpublished until 1684), binary arithmetic, calculating machine, logic, mining machinery. — In 1683 in Hanover and the Harz mines, building windmill pumps. Sought the post of imperial librarian in Vienna after Lambeck's death (1680). Reachable by letter.
- **Otto von Guericke**: former mayor of Magdeburg, inventor of the air pump. Knows: air pump, vacuum and air-pressure experiments, sulphur globe, weather glass. — Aged 80, living with his son in Hamburg since 1681; dies there in May 1686. Showed his experiments at the Regensburg Diet in 1654.
- **Christiaan Huygens**: mathematician and instrument maker. Knows: pendulum clock, balance spring, lens grinding, mechanics, probability, wave theory of light. — Back in The Hague since 1681, grinding long telescope lenses with his brother; publishes the tubeless 'aerial' telescope in 1684.
- **Denis Papin**: French Huguenot physician and experimenter, former assistant of Huygens and Boyle. Knows: air pump, steam digester with safety valve, gunpowder cylinder. — In Venice 1681–1684 directing experiments for a scientific academy; returns to the Royal Society in London in 1684.
- **Adam Adamandy Kochański SJ**: Jesuit mathematician, clockmaker, chaplain and librarian at the court of Jan III Sobieski. Knows: clocks and balance springs, geometry (approximation of pi, 1685), magnetism. — In Poland, in Sobieski's service since 1680; corresponds with Leibniz and Hevelius. Earlier taught at Jesuit colleges in the Empire and Bohemia.
- **Johannes Hevelius**: brewer, councillor and astronomer in Danzig. Knows: star positions, lunar maps, comets, large instruments with open sights. — In Danzig, rebuilding after the fire of 1679 destroyed his observatory. Friend of Sobieski; in 1684 names the constellation 'Sobieski's Shield' for the relief of Vienna.
- **Georg Rimpler**: Saxon-born fortress engineer, imperial lieutenant-colonel and chief of engineers since 1682. Knows: fortification, mining and counter-mining, siege geometry. — In Vienna, directing fortification and countermines; foresaw the attack between Burg and Löwel bastions. Wounded in the left arm on 25 July 1683, dies in the night of 2–3 August.
- **Christoph von Börner**: colonel commanding the artillery of the defence. Knows: gunnery, gun founding, powder, arsenal stores. — In Vienna throughout the siege. Controls the people a player needs for anything cast in bronze or bored.
- **Daniel Suttinger**: imperial captain and engineer. Knows: surveying, fortress plans, perspective city views. — In Vienna during the siege; afterwards draws the best-known plans of the city and the Ottoman siege works.
- **Count Ernst Rüdiger von Starhemberg**: city commandant of Vienna, commander of the defence. Knows: infantry command, fortress defence. — In Vienna throughout. Refuses the summons to surrender; ill with dysentery 11–20 August.
- **Count Zdenko Kaspar Kaplirs**: vice-president of the Hofkriegsrat, chairman of the college of deputies governing Vienna after the court leaves. Knows: administration, supply. — In Vienna throughout, aged 72; heads the civil government and supply beside Starhemberg. Made field marshal in late 1683.
- **Duke Charles V of Lorraine**: commander of the imperial field army, brother-in-law of Leopold I. Knows: field command. — Outside the city north of the Danube; reachable only by courier across the lines.
- **Jan III Sobieski**: king of Poland, ally by the treaty dated 31 March 1683. Knows: war against Ottomans and Tatars, cavalry. — In Poland until August; commands the relief army on 12 September.
- **Samuel Oppenheimer**: court factor and army contractor from Heidelberg, imperial war factor since 1679. Knows: credit, bills of exchange, army supply. — Lives in Vienna since 1674 by personal privilege although Jews were expelled in 1670.
- **Wilhelm von Schröder**: cameralist in imperial service, Fellow of the Royal Society (1662), took over the Kunst- und Werkhaus in 1677 (closed 1681). Knows: English science and manufactures, state finance. — In imperial service; where he spends the siege is not recorded. The Werkhaus burns in 1683. Publishes the Fürstliche Schatz- und Rentkammer in 1686; dies 1688.
- **Philipp Wilhelm von Hörnigk**: jurist and cameralist, brother-in-law of the late Johann Joachim Becher. Knows: trade statistics of the hereditary lands (with Becher from 1673), public law. — In imperial service around Vienna; whereabouts during the siege not recorded. Was secretary to the envoy Count Lamberg in Berlin (1680); writes 'Österreich über alles, wann es nur will' (1684).
- **Johann van Ghelen**: university printer since 1678, holder of the privilege for Latin and Italian newspapers (1678), five presses. Knows: printing, news trade. — In Vienna; takes part in the defence and writes an account of the siege that his firm spreads in Italy. Prints Abraham a Sancta Clara's Auff, auff, ihr Christen.
- **Georg Franz Kolschitzky**: interpreter and trader who knows Turkish. Knows: Ottoman language and customs. — In Vienna. Crosses the Ottoman lines as courier with his servant Michaelowitz on 13 August, returns on the 17th. His founding the first coffee house is legend.
- **Marco d'Aviano**: Capuchin preacher, papal legate with the relief army. Knows: preaching; trusted adviser of Leopold I. — Outside the city; joins the relief army and mediates between Sobieski and Charles of Lorraine at the council of war of 4 September.

## Events and timeline
- 1679: Great plague in Vienna; the court leaves, Sorbait is made Generalinquisitor, Leopold I vows a column on the Graben. Modern estimates of the dead start at about 12,000; contemporaries claimed far more (background).
- 1680: Sorbait's Pest-Ordnung and Abraham a Sancta Clara's Mercks Wienn are printed (background).
- 1680–1682 (background): the great comet of 1680–1681 and the comet of 1682 (later Halley's) are read in Vienna as omens of war.
- 1682 (background): Imre Thököly, with Ottoman backing, holds Upper Hungary; Caprara's embassy to prolong the Peace of Vasvár fails.
- 1682 (background): Acta Eruditorum, the first German learned journal, begins at Leipzig; Leibniz prints his series for pi in it.
- 1683: Jakob Bernoulli in Basel studies compound interest reckoned ever more often (the limit later called e).
- 1683: Blondel's L'art de jetter les bombes, on gunnery by Galileo's parabola, appears in Paris.
- 1683 Jan 26: defensive alliance of Leopold I with Elector Max Emanuel of Bavaria.
- 1683 Mar 31: alliance of Leopold I and Jan III Sobieski, dated 31 March (signed at Warsaw on 1 April), with papal backing: each helps if Vienna or Kraków is besieged. Days later the Ottoman army leaves Adrianople.
- 1683 Jul 7: cavalry clash at Petronell; that evening the emperor and court leave Vienna for Linz and Passau.
- 1683 Jul 9: Leopold appoints a college of deputies under Kaplirs to govern Vienna.
- 1683 Jul 10–13: about 11,000 imperial troops enter the city; some 5,000 citizens and volunteers join them.
- 1683 Jul 13: Starhemberg has the suburbs burned, except the Leopoldstadt, including the plague lazaretto on the Als, the tanners' and gardeners' quarters, mills and workshops.
- 1683 Jul 14: the Ottoman army closes round Vienna; a fire at the Schottenstift's farm threatens the powder magazine. No instruments, books, mercury or letters come in until 12 September.
- 1683 Jul 18: The Ottomans find and cut a water conduit running into the city from the suburbs.
- 1683 Jul 23 and 25: first Ottoman mines at the Burg ravelin and the Löwelbastei.
- 1683 Jul 25: the chief engineer Georg Rimpler is wounded in a sortie; his arm wound festers and he dies in the night of 2–3 August.
- 1683 Aug 1: Food prices are fixed by decree; the decree has to be repeated almost daily and is extended to medicines.
- 1683 c. Aug 8: The rote Ruhr (dysentery) breaks out in the city; Starhemberg is ill from 11 to 20 August.
- 1683 Aug 13–17: Kolschitzky carries messages to Charles of Lorraine and returns.
- 1683 Aug 27: first rocket signals at night from St Stephen's tower to the relief army; more follow on later nights.
- 1683 Aug 31: A hit behind the Löwelbastei sets a munitions store on fire and much of the powder reserve is lost.
- 1683 Sep 1–2: the ruined Burg ravelin is lost.
- 1683 Sep 3: Food runs short; sorties at the Schottentor bring in 22 oxen.
- 1683 Sep 4: a mine breaches the Burgbastei; the breach is sealed overnight. The same day the allied commanders hold their council of war at Stetteldorf near Tulln.
- 1683 Sep 9: Mayor Liebenberg dies of dysentery after weeks of illness.
- 1683 Sep 12: the relief army under Sobieski and Charles of Lorraine attacks from the Kahlenberg; the Ottoman army flees and the siege is raised.
- 1683 Sep: Louis XIV sends troops into the Spanish Netherlands.
- 1683 Sep 17: Leeuwenhoek writes from Delft to the Royal Society about animalcules in scrapings from teeth.
- 1683 Oct 9: allied victory at Párkány; Oct 27: Gran (Esztergom) surrenders.
- 1683 autumn: A typhus-like epidemic after the siege kills many residents.
- 1683 Dec 25: Kara Mustafa is strangled at Belgrade on the Sultan's order.
- 1684: Hevelius in Danzig names the constellation Scutum Sobiescianum.
- 1684: Hörnigk's 'Österreich über alles, wann es nur will' appears anonymously.
- 1684: Papin leaves Venice for London; Huygens publishes Astroscopia compendiaria on the tubeless telescope.
- 1684 Mar 5: Holy League of the emperor, Poland and Venice signed at Linz under papal patronage.
- 1684 Aug: Halley visits Newton in Cambridge and learns he has derived the planetary ellipse from an inverse-square force.
- 1684 Aug 15: Truce of Regensburg leaves Louis XIV his annexations, including Strasbourg, for twenty years.
- 1684 Oct: Leibniz's Nova methodus pro maximis et minimis, the first printed calculus, appears in the Acta Eruditorum.
- 1685 Jan 17 (outlook): Johannes Diodato receives the first privilege to serve coffee publicly in Vienna.

## Quest hooks
- Sorbait was not believed in 1678; he may listen to someone who explains how a sickness travels, and he has the standing to issue an order
- The Ruhr begins in August and fills the hospitals. Which wells stand next to which cesspits, and who can order water boiled when firewood is short?
- The death-inspection registers name each dead person's house and illness; put on a plan of the city, or drawn as a line through the siege weeks, they show the command what dysentery is doing
- Kollonitsch's emergency hospitals in the monasteries need rules for wounds, linen and latrines, and he can enforce them
- A wounded officer's arm is festering and the Feldscher wants to probe it again
- A spectacle maker and a scholar who has read of Leeuwenhoek's animalcules but never seen one
- Refuse, dung and dead horses cannot leave the walls; someone must decide where they go
- An abbot's garden with a strange tuber from the Indies that nobody eats
- Vintners sweeten sour wine with litharge, and a household has the colic
- After the relief, lice-ridden soldiers and refugees crowd the city and a new fever begins
- A barometer in a week: Idrija mercury from an apothecary, a yard of glass tube, and a Jesuit professor who denies the void must be shown the column.
- Starhemberg's lookout on St Stephen's has a poor spyglass; a better objective, or a second lens arrangement, earns a hearing with the command.
- The artillery colonel wants bombs to land where they are aimed: range tables from the parabola, corrected by trial shots, against the gunners' rules of thumb.
- Listening posts in cellars and water tubs detect Ottoman miners under the Burg bastion, which has no countermine galleries; the engineers need to fix direction and distance of the digging.
- Starhemberg's dispatches to Charles of Lorraine risk capture with every courier, and the rockets from the tower can only say "we still hold out": devise a cipher the clerks can use at speed, or a signal code that carries numbers and days.
- After the relief: write to Leibniz in Hanover or Guericke in Hamburg; a letter with one true new result (a series, a pump design) opens the republic of letters.
- The Hofkammer drowns in war accounts; a clockmaker could build an adding machine if someone explains the tens carry.
- The Schemnitz mines are flooding beyond what horses and water wheels can lift; the mine office will listen to anyone with a credible fire engine, but a year is short.
- Powder is running short after the magazine fire; new powder needs saltpetre, sulphur and a mill inside the walls
- Fixed prices have emptied the market stalls and filled the black market; the deputies ask what to do
- The Hofkammer cannot pay the garrison; Oppenheimer will advance money if someone can show him it will be repaid
- A printer's privilege and the Jesuit censors stand between the player and any printed sheet
- Schröder, a Fellow of the Royal Society whose Werkhaus closed in 1681 and burns in the siege, looks for a project the emperor will fund
- After the relief, Hörnigk collects figures for a book on how Austria could supply itself
